# Research notes on 1 Samuel 15

**What I couldn't find.** I ran out of searches before I could look at the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey, the Lutheran, Methodist and Assemblies of God sites, or any prosperity or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Those are left out, so section 3 covers only NET Bible notes and one passage from Augustine. Two pages I opened in full (Enduring Word and Precept Austin) were cut off part way: Enduring Word ends partway through v. 16, and Precept Austin's full text ends at v. 2, though search snippets from it reach later verses. Points from them have the URL but no exact citation.

**Labels.** I name a tradition only where the site or page shows it, or where you assigned the site to one.

---

## 1–2. Traditional reading, verse by verse, with differences noted

**v. 1:** Wiersbe (quoted by Precept Austin) sees this as God giving Saul "one more chance" to prove himself. Precept Austin points out that the Hebrew word *shama* ("listen/obey") is a key word, used 8 times in the chapter. Listening here means obeying: this is a command, not a suggestion. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)

**v. 2:** Guzik says the Amalekites were the first people to attack Israel after the escape from Egypt. They went after the weakest people, and time does not wipe out sin before God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/) Precept Austin notes that the title "LORD of hosts" shows God rules over nations, including wicked ones. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)

**v. 3:**
- Guzik: the Hebrew verb for "utterly destroy" appears seven times in the story, stressing total judgment. He adds that Christians under the New Covenant have a different calling (John 18:36). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)
- Ligonier: God is declaring that all the Amalekite people and all their possessions are to be "put under the ban," or "devoted" to Him. This is holy war. Saul is to be God's instrument to punish Amalek's sins, past and present (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/vengeance-on-amalek)
- BibleHub study notes: the ban (*herem*) indicates a complete consecration to God, often through destruction, so the plunder was not for anyone's personal gain. (https://biblehub.com/study/1_samuel/15-3.htm)
- MacArthur (via Precept Austin): God's judgment was severe on those who would destroy His people. It was equally severe to those who disobeyed (cf. Achan in Josh. 7:10–26) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)

**vv. 4–5:** Guzik says Saul was clearly a capable general who could raise a large army and time his attack. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/) The NET note says "lay in wait" follows the Greek and Latin versions. The standard Hebrew text instead reads "he contended." (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=15)

**v. 6:** Guzik: Saul showed wisdom and mercy in sparing the Kenites, because God's judgment was not aimed at them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)

**vv. 8–9:**
- Guzik quotes Poole: Saul may have spared Agag out of pity, respect for royalty, or to show off in his triumph. He quotes Maclaren: "Partial obedience is complete disobedience." Worthless things were destroyed only to save trouble.
- Guzik compares Israel's profiting from this war of judgment to a hangman emptying the pockets of the man he has just executed.
- He also quotes Meyer's spiritual reading, in which Agag stands for our urge to please ourselves, our pet sin. (all https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)
- NET note: the Hebrew for "fat calves" is difficult. The standard text reads "the second ones," which the Jewish commentator Kimchi took to mean second-born young. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=15)

**vv. 10–11** (main point of debate; see also v. 29):
- Matthew Henry: Repentance in God is not a change of mind, as it is in us, but a change of method. The change was in Saul (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/15-11.htm)
- Geneva Study Bible: God never changes or repents in his eternal plan, though he seems to us to repent when anything goes contrary to his temporal election. (same URL)
- Keil & Delitzsch: the word shows simply the sorrow of the divine love at the rebellion of sinners. Saul's real sin was wanting to be absolute ruler instead of the Lord's follower. (same URL)
- Guzik: this is God describing himself in human terms. God knew Saul's heart from the start, but he is not an unfeeling God "with a clipboard." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)
- Constable: God regretted that He had made Saul king because of Saul's decisions, not because God thought He had made a mistake by choosing Saul. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-15.html)
- Samuel's reaction: translations split between "distressed" or "grieved" (KJV, BSB) and "angry" (ESV, NIV, NASB, NET). (https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/15-11.htm)
- What Samuel prayed: the Pulpit Commentary takes it as an earnest prayer for forgiveness for Saul, and for a change in his heart. No change came, and since forgiveness depends on repentance, Saul was not forgiven. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/15-11.htm)

**v. 12:**
- Matthew Henry: Saul set up a monument at Carmel, seeking his own honour more than the honour of God (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_015.cfm)
- Guzik contrasts this with the shy Saul who hid among the baggage (10:22). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)
- NET note: the Greek translation adds a line saying Saul was offering the best of the plunder as burnt offerings. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=15)

**v. 13:** Guzik thinks Saul was self-deceived and probably believed his own claim. He quotes Maclaren: someone who had truly obeyed would have been slower to boast about it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)

**vv. 14–15:** Guzik counts four excuses: Saul blames the people, includes himself in the obedient part, justifies keeping the best, and claims a religious motive. He also notices the phrase "the LORD *your* God," as if the LORD was Samuel's God, not Saul's. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)

**v. 16:** Guzik: Saul's "Speak on" (BSB: "Tell me") shows his proud desire to retain some control. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)

**vv. 17–19:** BibleHub's chapter summary: Samuel exposes Saul's self-deception, setting his humble beginnings against his present rebellion. (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_samuel/15.htm) The NET translates v. 19 "greedily rushed upon the plunder." (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=15)

**vv. 20–21:** Matthew Henry: Saul repeats his vindication of himself, as that which, in defiance of conviction, he resolved to abide by (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_015.cfm)

**v. 22:** Enduring Word summary: religious practice without a surrendered, obedient heart means nothing to God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/) BibleHub: God values obedience over ritualistic offerings and that true worship involves aligning our hearts and actions with His will (https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/1_samuel/15.htm)

**v. 23:**
- Keil & Delitzsch (via Guzik): "All conscious disobedience is actually idolatry, because it makes self-will, the human I, into a god." (https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Sa/1Sa_15.cfm)
- Kingcomments goes further, linking rebellion with turning to demons and the occult. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-samuel-15.html)
- Precept Austin cites the Brown-Driver-Briggs Hebrew dictionary: the word for "arrogance" literally means "to display pushing." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)
- Matthew Henry: the verse is about not the rebellion of the people against their prince, but of a prince against God (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_015.cfm)
- Guzik: the rejection was final but not immediate. Almost 25 years passed before another king was enthroned. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)

**vv. 24–25:**
- Matthew Henry: Saul's confession was not free nor ingenuous, but extorted by the rack (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_015.cfm)
- Pulpit Commentary: the verse shows the gap between bare conviction and true repentance. "I feared the people" is an excuse tacked straight on, and the only pardon Saul wanted was relief from the penalty. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/1-samuel-15.html)
- Precept Austin calls it a confession without repentance (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)

**v. 26:** Precept Austin: Why would Samuel want to return and participate in sham worship with Saul? (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)

**vv. 27–28:**
- Guzik: As useless as the torn piece of robe was in his hand, so now his leadership of the nation was futile. Now he ruled against God, not for Him. Just as the robe tore because Saul grasped it too tightly, so his tight grip on pride and stubbornness meant the kingdom would be taken away from him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)
- Kingcomments: the "neighbor" is not named, but we know it is David. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-samuel-15.html)

**v. 29** (how vv. 11, 29 and 35 fit together):
- **Classical view (Reformed and Baptist sites):**
  - Kevin DeYoung (TGC): God's regret is not analogous in every way to our regret. This seems to be the point verse 29 is explicitly making. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/kevin-deyoung/does-god-have-regret/)
  - John Piper (Desiring God): For God to say, "I feel sorrow that I made Saul king," is not the same as saying, "I would not make him king if I had it to do over." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-does-not-repent-like-a-man)
- **Open theism:** Don Stewart describes this view (he doesn't hold it): God really regretted the decision, which supposedly shows that God takes risks and sometimes these risks are regretted. Stewart rejects it and reads v. 11 in light of v. 29. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/does-god-know-everything/25-did-the-lord-regret-making-saul-king.cfm)
- **Middle position (NET note, from Robert Chisholm's work):** v. 29 marks v. 28 as an unchangeable decree. But this does not mean that God never deviates from his stated intentions or changes his mind. On the contrary, several passages describe him as changing his mind. In fact, his willingness to do so is one of his fundamental divine attributes (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=15)
- Constable: Samuel reminded the king that Yahweh was the "Glory of Israel." Saul wanted the glory for himself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/15-15.html)

**v. 30:** Pulpit Commentary: Saul is asking for the honor his rank still deserves, and Samuel agrees because Saul remained king in practice. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-15.html) Chuck Smith paraphrases the request as "Make me look good in front of the people, I've sinned." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/15-12.html)

**v. 31:**
- Guzik: going back with Saul did not win back the kingdom, but it may have moved Saul's heart closer to God for his soul's sake. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-15/)
- Why Samuel went back: Because God had not raised up Saul's replacement yet, and Saul was better than the anarchy that would come with no king. (https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_1Sa/1Sa_15.cfm)
- Pulpit Commentary sees in it pity for the fallen king. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/1-samuel-15.html)

**v. 32:** NET note (a real text issue): the Hebrew word translated "cheerfully" is rare and unclear. NET takes it as "trembling," following the Greek translation. It also judges "is past" to be a copying error, so Agag says "Surely death is bitter!" In that reading he knows he is about to die, rather than thinking he is safe (KJV, NIV, BSB). (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=15)

**v. 33:** Pulpit Commentary: Samuel's act on the king's body showed the people how serious the divine command was, and it must have given pain to the prophet's mind. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-15.html)

**vv. 34–35:**
- Adam Clarke: Saul visiting Samuel later (19:22–24) doesn't contradict this. From now on Samuel never again acknowledged him as king, but he mourned and prayed for him. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)
- Matthew Henry: Samuel mourned for Saul's everlasting state, having no hopes of bringing him to repentance. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_015.cfm)
- Pulpit Commentary: "Samuel mourned for Saul, but we do not hear that Saul mourned for himself." (https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/1-samuel-15.html)

**Across the chapter: was Saul saved?** Evangelical writers disagree.
- Constable: Saul did not lose his salvation because he failed to obey God completely, but he did lose his opportunity to serve God (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-15.html)
- Life Application Bible (via Precept Austin): God wasn't rejecting Saul as a person, but it was too late to get the kingdom back. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-15-commentary)
- GotQuestions (quoted on Precept Austin) won't decide: Saul's salvation rests with God, not with us. (same URL)
- Matthew Henry (above) and BibleHub's survey lean the other way. BibleHub says many see Saul as likely unsaved, while a minority point to his admissions of guilt (15:24–25). (https://biblehub.com/q/is_king_saul_considered_saved.htm)

## 3. Other views (limited)

- **Augustine, quoted by Bishop Wordsworth (Anglican)** on v. 11: God feels no remorse and is never deceived. When Scripture says he "repents," expect a change in what he does: He changed Saul's kingdom when it is said He repented of making him king. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/15-11.htm)
- **NET Bible notes:** see vv. 5, 9, 12, 29 and 32 above.
- **A modern use of the text:** Peter Leithart (TGC) compares Amalekite warfare with Hamas's October 7 attack. He also makes clear that Hamas isn't Amalek. Hamas isn't literally under Yahweh's ban and curse. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/hamas-tactics-amalekites/)
